title: How to teach kids in the age of AI, from a top LA teacher
gist: Conrad Hughes, head of the International School of Los Angeles, argues that evidence of cognitive offloading (falling PISA scores, MIT LLM brain-activity research, rising 'hasty reading') calls for cognitively demanding pedagogies — handwriting, paper reading, oral exams, debate — alongside intentional, curated AI use rather than outright bans.

insights.claim: Falling PISA scores in reading, maths and science have been linked to chatbot use, raising concerns that students are cognitively offloading thinking to AI.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Evidence of AI-driven learning loss could trigger regulatory and procurement backlash against classroom AI products.
insights.quote: Falling PISA scores in reading, maths and science have been linked to chatbot use, raising concerns about cognitive offloading.

insights.claim: Studies such as MIT's research on brain activity when using large language models for essay writing, plus OECD-published PISA declines, have focused attention on the harmful effects of over-reliance on technology in classrooms.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Academic evidence against LLM over-use strengthens the narrative risk for edtech AI vendors.
insights.locator: The ability to flourish with technology

insights.claim: 'Hasty reading' — children reading quickly but inaccurately — is described as skyrocketing.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Signals measurable deterioration in foundational literacy that may shape education policy and spending priorities.
insights.quote: "Hasty reading" (when children read quickly but inaccurately) is skyrocketing

insights.claim: The author argues that standards of criticality and cognitive acumen are dropping, making intentional, cognitively demanding teaching essential.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Frames a societal skills-erosion risk with long-run implications for workforce quality.
insights.quote: In a world where the standards of criticality and cognitive acumen are dropping

insights.claim: Cognitively demanding pedagogies — handwritten notes, reading from the page, oral exams and debate — are emerging as a key strategy to keep students thinking for themselves in the AI era.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Points to demand shifts toward low-tech, assessment and in-person teaching formats rather than pure screen-based edtech.

insights.claim: Reading, writing, manual and mental problem solving, project-based learning and in-class assessments exercise fluid-intelligence subcomponents — working memory, pattern recognition and processing speed — rather than letting AI do the work.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Defines the skills schools will prioritise, shaping curriculum and assessment design markets.

insights.claim: Debate, oral examinations, vivas and discussion-based learning are increasingly necessary because face-to-face interaction is being de-skilled as so much activity moves online.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Shift to oral and in-class assessment undermines AI-cheating risk and changes how credentials are validated.
insights.quote: there is a clear de-skilling of face-to-face interaction

insights.claim: Numeracy and literacy are the main vehicles for CDPs: notes should be handwritten, books read on paper with comprehension tests, mental arithmetic done without technology, and memory tested frequently.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Suggests sustained demand for print materials and non-digital assessment in schools.

insights.claim: Parents should read to children at night until at least age 11 and engage them in discussions that push vocabulary and syntax.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Highlights home learning as a lever, relevant to children's publishing and family education markets.

insights.claim: Much of the new approach is a return to basics — pen and paper, unaided problem-solving, oral communication and books — which would have been seen as archaic twenty years ago but now are seen as necessary for the future.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Reversal of the decades-long edtech digitisation thesis in classrooms is a notable sentiment shift.
insights.quote: Twenty years ago, arguably, these would have been seen as archaic, whereas today they are seen as necessary for the future.
insights.locator: Going back to basics to move forward

insights.claim: Integration of technology including AI in classrooms should be intentional rather than de facto, with an explicit educational vision and weighing of benefits and drawbacks for each use.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Favors edtech vendors whose products demonstrate clear pedagogical purpose over generic AI tools.
insights.quote: The integration of technology in the classroom, including AI, needs to be intentional and not de facto.
insights.locator: The integration of technology in the classroom

insights.claim: AI tutors should be vetted and curated by an education expert, and internet-access assignments should be designed assuming students will use AI.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Implies a curation/vetting layer and AI-aware assessment design become requirements for AI tutor adoption.
insights.quote: AI tutors, for example, need to be vetted and curated by an education expert
insights.locator: The integration of technology in the classroom

insights.claim: Banning AI and phones in schools is described as the least interesting response, because it is what schools actively do, not what they prohibit, that matters.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Suggests outright bans are not the endpoint; demand for AI literacy and curated tools persists.
insights.quote: The least interesting approach to this paradigm shift, or perhaps paradigm return, is to ban and prohibit

insights.claim: Students should be taught about algorithm design, social media's emotional hooks, the environmental effects of AI, and 'how to think to prompt' rather than 'prompting to think'.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Points to growing curriculum demand for data, AI and ethics literacy content.
insights.quote: how to think to prompt (as opposed to prompting to think)
insights.locator: At the same time, we should

insights.claim: If schools focus on CDPs, screens and AI become less important and students using them will likely be more discerning; the goal is preparing students to use technology well rather than keeping them away.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Suggests a more selective, quality-driven long-term demand for educational AI rather than wholesale adoption.
insights.locator: If we focus on these things
